meta.method: Every row was built by reading castandards.json's paraphrase against csta2017.json's paraphrase (itself written straight from CSTA's own text, never from CA's) side by side -- not by matching code numbers, which turn out not to line up reliably once CA's 9-12 band merges CSTA's separate Level 3A and 3B. A CA code can appear more than once when it genuinely compresses more than one CSTA standard into a single statement; a CSTA code with no row here has no honest CA counterpart (most of Level 3B falls in that category, since CA's core 9-12 set only draws from Level 3A's AP strand and a handful of 3B's other standards). Consumed by assets/js/standards-coverage.js to drive the coverage map's cross-framework compare-text feature.

strength_definitions.strong: same claim, close enough in wording and scope that the two are teaching the same thing
strength_definitions.partial: same general topic, but one side's phrasing adds, drops, or reframes something the other doesn't say
strength_definitions.related: adjacent territory -- worth surfacing, but close reading shows they are not actually the same standard

crosswalk.note: Same standard: recommending device-design improvements from watching how users interact with it.
Same standard: combining hardware and software components to collect and exchange data.
Same standard, including CSTA's own point that a problem may be in a connected device rather than the device itself.
Same standard: modeling the role of protocols in transmitting data across a network.

CA's paraphrase frames this around choosing a countermeasure for a given threat. CSTA's actual standard is the more descriptive ask of explaining how physical and digital security measures protect information, without yet requiring students to weigh threats against each other.
Same standard: combining multiple encryption methods to model secure transmission.
Same standard: representing the same data with multiple encoding schemes.
Same standard: transforming collected data to make it more useful and reliable.

CA's paraphrase leans on a change-one-variable-at-a-time framing. CSTA's actual standard is about refining a model against the data it generated, without that controlled-variable emphasis specifically.
Same standard: using flowcharts or pseudocode to work out an algorithm before writing real code.
Same standard: naming variables clearly enough that the operations on them make sense.
Same standard: combining nested loops and compound conditionals, developed iteratively.
Same standard: decomposing a problem into subproblems to make a program easier to build and review.
Same standard: procedures with parameters, reusable across inputs.
Same standard, close to verbatim: seeking and incorporating feedback from teammates and users.
Same standard: reusing existing code, media, or libraries with attribution.
Same standard: testing with a deliberate range of test cases, not just the expected one.
Same standard: distributing tasks and keeping a shared timeline on a team project.
Same standard: documenting a program so someone else can follow, test, and debug it.
Same standard: weighing the tradeoffs of a computing technology's effect on daily life and careers.
Same standard: discussing bias and accessibility problems in existing technology's design.
Same standard: collaborating with many contributors, e.g. through crowdsourcing, on a computational artifact.

Numbering shifts here: CA's IC.24 (public-vs-private-information tradeoff) is CSTA's 2-IC-23. CA's own IC.23 slot went to an added licensing standard with no Level 2 counterpart -- see that entry's note in castandards.json, and its absence from this crosswalk.
Same standard: abstractions hiding a computing system's implementation details inside an everyday object.
Same standard: application software, system software, and hardware as interacting layers of abstraction.
Same standard: writing down a systematic troubleshooting process so someone else can use it.

CA's NI.4 (organizational performance demands: latency, bandwidth, throughput) is actually the Level 3B standard on network-functionality issues (bandwidth, load, delay, topology), not a Level 3A one -- CA folded a Level 3B standard into a lower-numbered slot when it merged 3A and 3B into one 9-12 band.

CA's NI.5 (address lookup and routing letting the internet scale and stay reliable) is CSTA's 3A-NI-04 (routers, switches, servers, topology, addressing) -- the numbers are effectively swapped relative to NI.4/3B-NI-03 above, an artifact of merging 3A and 3B into one band.

CA compresses three CSTA cybersecurity standards into one general "different threats, different defenses, real tradeoff" statement: recommending measures by efficiency/feasibility/ethics (this one, 3A-NI-06), comparing usability-vs-security tradeoffs (3A-NI-07), and explaining tradeoffs when implementing a recommendation (3A-NI-08).
See the note on 3A-NI-06 -- CA's NI.6 also covers this usability-vs-security-tradeoffs standard.
See the note on 3A-NI-06 -- CA's NI.6 also covers this tradeoffs-of-implementation standard.

CA's NI.7 is specifically about symmetric-vs-asymmetric encryption tradeoffs, a claim CSTA's own 9-12 standards never actually state (public-key encryption appears only as a Level 2/6-8 example). The closest CSTA standard in the same Cybersecurity subconcept is 3A-NI-05, on how malware and other attacks affect sensitive data, but it is not the same claim.
Same standard: translating a real-world thing between different bit representations.
Same standard, down to the same tradeoff list: cost, speed, reliability, accessibility, privacy, integrity.

CA frames this around a visualization being a design choice that shapes what people take away from it -- a persuasion/interpretation emphasis. CSTA's 3A-DA-11 frames the same activity around using software tools to help others understand a real-world phenomenon -- a tool-use emphasis.

CA's DA.11 (checking a model against real observations and adjusting it) matches 3A-DA-12's own clarifying text about validating a model against real-world data, but CSTA's 3B-DA-07 (evaluating a model's or simulation's ability to test a hypothesis) covers closely related territory that CA doesn't index separately.

CA's AP.12 frames this as combining a known algorithm with one you design yourself. CSTA's 3A-AP-13 is about building prototypes from prior knowledge and personal interest -- related, but CA adds a "combine known + new" framing CSTA doesn't state.
Same standard: lists replacing a pile of separately named variables.
Same standard: justifying a control-structure choice on implementation, readability, and performance tradeoffs.
Same standard: events initiating instructions in an iteratively developed artifact.
Same standard: decomposing a problem into procedures, modules, or objects.
Same standard: an artifact built from procedures, data-plus-procedures, or interrelated programs.
Same standard, close to verbatim: systematically designing for broad audiences using their feedback.
Same standard: evaluating licenses that restrict use of a library or other resource.
Same standard, with CA adding "performance" to the list of what testing improves; CSTA's own wording names usability and accessibility only.
Same standard: designing in team roles using collaborative tools.
Same standard: documenting design decisions in whatever form fits, for a complex program.
CA drops "ethical" from CSTA's list of practices computing impacts, otherwise the same standard.
Same standard: testing and refining an artifact to reduce bias and equity deficits.
Same standard: one algorithm applying to problems across more than one discipline.

CA's IC.26 ("critically examine how new technologies reshape social, economic, and political structures") doesn't match any single CSTA standard cleanly -- it reads as a blend of 3B-IC-25 (evaluate an artifact's net benefit and harm to society), 3B-IC-26 (evaluate equity, access, and influence in the global distribution of computing resources), and 3B-IC-27 (predict how computing innovations might evolve), none of which CA otherwise indexes.
See the note on 3B-IC-25 -- CA's IC.26 also gestures at this equity/access/influence standard.
See the note on 3B-IC-25 -- CA's IC.26 also gestures at this predict-how-innovations-evolve standard.
Same standard, close to verbatim, and coincidentally the same number: collaboration tools connecting people across cultures and career fields.
Same standard, same number: intellectual property law's beneficial and harmful effects on innovation.
Same standard, same number: privacy concerns from data collected automatically, without users noticing.
Same standard, same number: evaluating privacy's social and economic implications in a safety/law/ethics context.
